name: Adam Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a senior lineman on a crew covering the mountain district for the power company, out of the Pine Gap service yard. Most days it's maintenance on lines that run up through the hollows, replacing poles the woodpeckers have had, and clearing trees off conductors. Then a couple of times a year a big storm rolls through and we work sixteen-hour days for a week straight. I like knowing that the old lady at the top of Cutter's Ridge has heat because of us. What wears me out is the hours away from home in storm season, and the new rules that come down from the city every year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Ruth runs the office at our church, and we've got two kids, a boy who's twelve and a girl who's nine. We have a mortgage on the house, and twenty acres up the valley that came down from my grandfather, with a few head of cattle on it. I'm a deacon at church, I coach kids' baseball in the spring. I don't use any of these AI things. If I need to know something, I ask a man who's done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never believed a word of it. Folks in the city get excited about every new toy. I'd probably say that after church, over coffee, and folks would agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my life goes on like it has, and that suits me fine. The mountain doesn't care about computers. I'd still be climbing, and my boy might follow me into the trade one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep working, keep paying down the mortgage, keep the cattle fed. Put a bit more into savings like we always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your boy might follow you. Would you want that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would. It's honest work, it pays well, and you're doing something folks need. My granddad strung the first line up our valley in 1952, and I'd like a Weber still climbing it in 2052.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by new rules from the city?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Head office keeps adding forms and apps for things we've done right for years. Last year they wanted us to log every tree trim with a photo on a tablet. Half the hollows don't have signal, so we're taking pictures we can't send.

S0.say: I never believed a word of it, because city folks get excited about every new toy. I'd say that after church over coffee and folks would agree.
S0.think: My life goes on like it has, and that suits me fine, because the mountain doesn't care about computers. I'd still be climbing and my boy might follow me into the trade.
S0.do: Keeps working, paying down the mortgage and feeding the cattle as always. Puts a bit more into savings as usual.
S0.quote: My granddad strung the first line up our valley in 1952, and I'd like a Weber still climbing it in 2052.
S0.fieldNote: Adam's identity is tied to family, faith and the line his grandfather built. He resents rules handed down from head office more than he fears technology. His hope that his son follows him is central to how he sees the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say be careful about trusting machines over men who know the work. I'd tell the young guys to learn their trade properly, not lean on gadgets. And I'd say we don't need the government stepping in with handouts, we need companies to keep training people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me some. I don't use these tools and I don't plan to. If the company starts using them to decide where we go and what we fix, I'll be working for a machine, and I don't care for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job, and if the company forced a new tool on us, I'd learn just enough. I'd put more aside, maybe pay the mortgage down faster. I'd talk to my pastor and a couple of the older men at church about what they've seen with changes like this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like weather coming over the ridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd talk to your pastor. What would you hope he'd say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That a man's worth isn't his job, it's how he lives. I know that, I just need reminding sometimes. I'd want him to tell me the Lord didn't make me to take orders from a phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you seen a change like this before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the mill closed in 2009, half the men at church lost work. The ones who got through had family, land or a trade. I've got all three, which is why I'm uneasy, not scared.

S1.say: Be careful trusting machines over men who know the work, and learn your trade properly instead of leaning on gadgets. We don't need government handouts; companies should keep training people.
S1.think: It worries me some, because I don't use these tools and don't plan to. If the company uses them to decide where we go and what we fix, I'll be working for a machine, and I don't care for that.
S1.do: Keeps doing his job and learns only what the company forces on him. Saves more and pays the mortgage down faster, and talks with his pastor and older church members about past changes.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like weather coming over the ridge.
S1.quote: I'd want him to tell me the Lord didn't make me to take orders from a phone.
S1.fieldNote: Adam frames the threat as a question of dignity: taking orders from a machine. His memory of the 2009 mill closure gives him a model of who survives: those with family, land and a trade. He turns to church, not government or union, for support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when a few rich men at the tech companies decide for everyone else. I'd say it plain at church and to anyone who'd listen. And I'd say families and churches need to look after each other, because the government won't do it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd hit me hard. I'm not going to become a robot man at forty-three. Two years is no time at all to plan, and if they can put a robot up a pole in the hollows, then I'm out, senior or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd sit down with Ruth and work out how long we can go on savings and the cattle. We'd cut back on anything extra, no new truck, no trip to the coast. I'd keep working as long as they'd have me, and if I lost it, I'd lean on the land and on folks at church while I figured out what's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying a lot, and sleeping less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That God's still in charge and we're going to be all right. I'd mean it, mostly. I'd tell my boy to learn to fix what the robots can't, but I'd be lying if I said I knew what that was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on the land. Could the land actually keep you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not fully, not with a mortgage. A few head of cattle and a garden helps, but it's not a paycheck. It would buy us time and keep food on the table, and that counts for something.

S2.say: This is what happens when a few rich men at the tech companies decide for everyone else. Families and churches need to look after each other, because the government won't do it right.
S2.think: It would hit me hard, because I'm not becoming a robot man at forty-three. Two years is no time to plan, and if they can put a robot up a pole in the hollows, I'm out, senior or not.
S2.do: Works out with his wife how long savings and the cattle can carry the family and cuts extras like a new truck and a coastal trip. Keeps working as long as possible, then leans on the land and his church while working out next steps.
S2.feel: Alarmed, praying more and sleeping less.
S2.quote: I'd tell my boy to learn to fix what the robots can't, but I'd be lying if I said I knew what that was.
S2.fieldNote: Adam blames a handful of tech billionaires rather than government or his employer. His faith and land are his anchors, but he's honest that neither replaces a paycheck. His refusal to retrain leaves him with few active moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say same as before, but with five years folks have time to get their houses in order. Pay off debt, keep family close, don't count on the government. I'd say it at church and on the kids' baseball bleachers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is better. I'd be forty-eight, and we could pay off a lot more of the house by then. I still wouldn't learn the robot stuff, but I might look at what else I could do with my hands, maybe expand the cattle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw every spare bit of money at the mortgage, and maybe buy a few more cattle and fence the back ten acres. I'd keep working at the power company as long as possible. If they offered an apprenticeship-style course on robot repair, I might take it, but only if it was hands-on and local.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might expand the cattle. Is that a real plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. I've run numbers on the back of an envelope, and twenty head would pay for themselves, not much more. The cows won't replace my paycheck, but they won't be replaced by a robot either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ruth say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say trust God and do the work, which is what she always says. She'd be the one keeping the budget straight. She's better at that than me.

S3.say: With five years, folks have time to get their houses in order: pay off debt, keep family close and don't count on the government. I'd say it at church and on the kids' baseball bleachers.
S3.think: Five years is better, because at forty-eight we could have paid off much more of the house. I still wouldn't learn the robot stuff, but I might do more with my hands, maybe expand the cattle.
S3.do: Puts every spare bit of money on the mortgage and buys a few more cattle and fences the back ten acres. Keeps working at the power company and would consider a hands-on, local robot-repair course.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadier, with a plan.
S3.quote: The cows won't replace my paycheck, but they won't be replaced by a robot either.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Adam turns to land and debt, things he can see and touch. His cattle plan is modest and he knows it, but it gives him a sense of control. He would only consider retraining if it's hands-on and local, in the apprenticeship style he trusts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for people to prepare, so there's no excuse to be caught out. Teach your kids a trade, keep your family close, stay out of debt. I'd say government shouldn't be paying people to sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a lot better for me. I'd be fifty-three, the house could be near paid off, and I could keep working most of it. My worry is more for my boy, who'd be twenty-two and right at the start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working and paying down the house, and build up the cattle slowly. I'd steer my boy toward a trade that needs a person, maybe one where he works for himself. If the company offered a proper apprenticeship on the new machines, I'd sign up around year five or six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can live with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What trade would you steer your boy toward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something where folks have to trust the man doing it. Maybe running his own outfit, fixing whatever the robots break. I don't want him working for a robot; I'd rather he owned one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said government shouldn't pay people to sit at home. What if neighbours of yours needed that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the church would help first, like we did in 2009. I'm not saying nobody needs help. I'm saying a check in the mail isn't the same as a man feeling useful.

S4.say: Ten years is enough time to prepare, so there's no excuse to be caught out: teach your kids a trade, keep family close and stay out of debt. Government shouldn't be paying people to sit at home.
S4.think: Ten years is a lot better for me, since at fifty-three the house could be nearly paid off and I'd have worked most of the decade. My worry is more for my boy, who'd be twenty-two and just starting.
S4.do: Keeps working, pays down the house and builds up the cattle herd slowly. Steers his son toward a self-employed trade and would sign up for a company apprenticeship on the new machines around year five or six.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but able to live with it.
S4.quote: I don't want him working for a robot; I'd rather he owned one.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Adam's attention shifts to his son, and he moves from wanting him to work for a robot to wanting him to own one. His traditional views come through in preferring church help over government checks. He would accept retraining only in apprenticeship form, later in the decade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years, no time to pay off the house or plan, and I'd have nothing to fall back on but cattle and church. What would help is the company keeping senior men on to train whatever comes next, and proper apprenticeships, paid, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith, and that's what holds a lot of us together out here. When the mill shut, it wasn't the government that fed our neighbours, it was the church kitchen on Wednesday nights.

headlineQuote: When the mill shut, it wasn't the government that fed our neighbours, it was the church kitchen on Wednesday nights.
portrait: Adam Weber is a 43-year-old senior lineman covering the mountain district out of the Pine Gap service yard, a church deacon and kids' baseball coach with a wife who runs the church office, two children, a mortgage and twenty inherited acres with cattle. He never uses AI and trusts experience over gadgets. He's content in the hype scenario, uneasy about taking orders from machines in the gradual one, and alarmed when AGI comes in two years. With more time he pays down the house, builds up his cattle and plans for his son to run his own business. He blames a few tech billionaires and wants churches, families and paid apprenticeships to carry people through, not government handouts.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years leaves no time to pay off the house or plan, with only cattle and church to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping senior lineworkers on to train whatever comes next, and paid apprenticeships rather than handouts.
